title: The finger and the moon
hookLine: a teaching points at something, so don't stare at the pointing finger (a Buddhist image, Surangama Sutra, much used in Zen)

cards: Point across the room at a ball, for a small child or a puppy, and sometimes all they look at is your finger. They grab it, even.
The ball sits there, ignored, while they stare at your hand, waiting for it to do something. It's sweet in a toddler. It's less funny when grown-ups do it, with words and books instead of hands.
There's an old picture for this in the Buddhist world, and Zen teachers took it up. Someone points at the moon. And the other person looks at the finger.

teach.b: The picture appears in a Mahayana Buddhist scripture called the Surangama Sutra. The Buddha is talking with his cousin and attendant Ananda, who, tradition says, had heard a great many teachings and could recall them.
And the Buddha tells him, more or less: when someone points at the moon to show it to you, follow the finger and look at the moon.

teach.h: YOU LOSE THE MOON AND THE FINGER.
teach.b: If you look at the finger and take it for the moon, you lose the moon. And you lose the finger too, because you've mistaken what a finger is for. That last part is sharp.
A finger is for looking past. Zen took this image and ran with it.
A later Chan story tells of the teacher Huineng, who, tradition says, couldn't read, being asked by a nun how he could understand scriptures he couldn't even read.
The older sources have him answer that the truth doesn't depend on written words, and popular retellings put this picture in his mouth: the truth is like the moon, and words are like a finger.
You can see the moon without the finger. Here's why it matters beyond Zen. Every teaching points.
Words, books, rituals, even these lessons. They're fingers. They're precious, and worth studying, and they are not the thing.
The danger is falling in love with the pointing: memorizing the words, arguing about the finger's shape, collecting fingers, and missing the moon, which is right there, and was the point.
So when you hear a teaching, ask: what is this pointing at?

how: Zen teachers use the finger and the moon to remind students that sutras, koans and talks point toward direct experience, and study in Zen is paired with sitting practice.

games.q: someone points at the moon to show it to you. where do you look?
o: along the finger, at the moon.
games.why: follow the finger to the moon. take the finger for the moon, the sutra says, and you lose both.

practice: Put this phone face down, and if you can, go to a window or step outside and look up: clouds, blue, gray, the moon if you're lucky, a ceiling if that's all there is. This lesson was the finger; the sky is the moon.
Just look, and let it be bigger than anything you've read today.

wordCard.voice: Zhǐ yuè, Chinese for pointing at the moon, the name Chinese Buddhism gives this image: don't stare at the finger and miss the moon.

orig.note: Chinese, zhǐ yuè: pointing at the moon, the short name Chinese Buddhism uses for this image.

carryVoice: Your line: not the finger. The moon was the point all along. Forty-eight down.
